section_summary: This section contains reports, complaints, military-intelligence memoranda, cross-reference sheets, and newspaper clippings concerning alleged Japanese espionage, reconnaissance, and propaganda in the United States from 1931 through early 1934. Reports focus on maps and photographs of waterways, highways, railroads, bridges, industrial plants, shipyards, naval facilities, and the Panama Canal, while other documents discuss Japanese speakers, cultural outreach, and propaganda relating to Manchuria. State, War, Navy, and Justice Department officials repeatedly assess the credibility and legal significance of these allegations, including possible action against Lieutenant T. Arima and five Japanese railway engineers detained at Kearny, New Jersey.

subfiles.title: Lancaster report of a Japanese cadet's Chehalis River map
subfiles.about: Reports that a Japanese training-ship student displayed a detailed, apparently scaled map of the Chehalis River and nearby cities.
subfiles.summary: Lancaster says the map showed water lines, locations, distances, streets, and other unusual details extending well upriver from Aberdeen. He forwards the observation because of its possible security significance.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Lancaster's map report
subfiles.from: Maxwell M. Hamilton, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Lancaster's report concerning a detailed map displayed by a Japanese training-ship student.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton thanks Lancaster for directing the Department's attention to the reported map of parts of the Chehalis River. The reply offers no substantive assessment or proposed action.

subfiles.title: DeVaughn allegation of a Japanese water-poisoning plan
subfiles.about: Revives an earlier allegation that Japan planned to poison West Coast water supplies in the event of war.
subfiles.summary: DeVaughn claims confidential sources in Baja California disclosed the plan in 1926 or 1927 and that the information reached Secretary Kellogg. He urges federal protection of water sources in the western United States and Canada.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of DeVaughn's water-supply warning
subfiles.from: Maxwell M. Hamilton, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Acknowledges DeVaughn's suggestion that western water supplies be protected.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton states that the Department has noted DeVaughn's comments and appreciates his interest. The reply neither endorses the allegation nor identifies any action taken.

subfiles.title: Howe forwarding letter and enclosures
subfiles.about: Forwards a carbon letter and newspaper clipping concerning Japan and American policy in the Far East.
subfiles.summary: The surviving page consists mainly of Howe's business letterhead and State Department routing stamps. The contents are identified more fully in the Department's acknowledgment on page 8.

subfiles.title: Howe letter to David MacHaffie
subfiles.about: Discusses the Sino-Japanese crisis and warnings that the United States should guard against Japanese military ambitions.
subfiles.summary: After personal greetings and comments on Vermont weather, Howe notes reports of possible British and American involvement in defense of China's integrity. He repeats a warning attributed to Mrs. MacHaffie's mother that Japan had long been building a war machine for possible conflict.

subfiles.title: Clipping on the Burnetts' Japanese art exhibition
subfiles.about: Reports an exhibition of Japanese art collected by Lieutenant Colonel and Mrs. Burnett during their years in Japan.
subfiles.summary: The principal article describes tapestries, brocades, kimonos, and ceremonial robes lent to the Fleming Museum by Frances Hawes Cameron Burnett. It also recounts Charles Burnett's service as a language officer and military attaché and the couple's work as advisers to the American delegation at the London Naval Conference; unrelated newspaper columns remain visible on the page.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Howe's forwarding letter
subfiles.from: Maxwell M. Hamilton, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Howe's letter, clipping, and carbon letter concerning the Sino-Japanese dispute.
subfiles.summary: The Department notes that the White House referred Howe's January 30 communication. Hamilton thanks Howe for his interest in the Far Eastern situation and for furnishing the enclosures.

subfiles.title: Rudy report on visiting Japanese railway officials
subfiles.to: Oriental Relations, U.S. Department of State
subfiles.about: Reports the movements and contacts of Japanese railway official M. Inoue and K Line representative Kaname A. Suzuki.
subfiles.summary: Rudy says he met the two men through Esperanto and found them unwilling to seek publicity or address public groups. He supplies Inoue's anticipated itinerary and the names of Washington Esperantists to whom he referred him.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Rudy's report
subfiles.from: Maxwell M. Hamilton, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Acknowledges information about M. Inoue's visit to the United States.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton thanks Rudy for informing the Department about the general passenger agent's presence. The Department makes no accusation or request for further inquiry.

subfiles.title: White complaint about Japanese-language photograms
subfiles.about: Objects to the transmission of telegrams in Japanese by means of photograms and argues that this creates a security risk.
subfiles.summary: The surviving OCR is fragmentary, but White questions why Japanese residents or visitors should enjoy communications privileges that Americans cannot understand. The letter warns that such communications could become dangerous if relations with Japan deteriorated and appears to include a newspaper clipping.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of White's photogram complaint
subfiles.from: Maxwell M. Hamilton, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Acknowledges White's letter and enclosure concerning Japanese-language photograms.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton states that the letter and newspaper clipping were read with interest. He thanks White for sending the material but offers no policy response.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Japanese activities in Mexico
subfiles.about: Points to a memorandum presented to Mexico's foreign minister concerning Japanese activities and U.S. interests.
subfiles.summary: The sheet redirects the reader to file 894.20212/317. It describes the referenced item as a memorandum on Japanese activities in Mexico and their relation to the welfare of the United States.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to War Department report on H. E. Palmer
subfiles.about: Points to a report about Japanese military activities in the United States and H. E. Palmer.
subfiles.summary: The file note redirects researchers to 894.20212/319. No substantive report is reproduced on this page.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Japanese drug-firm activity in Mexico
subfiles.about: Indexes a report on Kinnosuke Sudo's promotional activities for a Japanese drug company in northern Mexico.
subfiles.summary: The note says Sudo conducted an extensive and expensive campaign in El Porvenir. It adds that the United States issued him a nonimmigrant visa to facilitate travel among northern Mexican cities.

subfiles.title: Donisoge allegations of Japanese covert operations
subfiles.about: Speculates that a Japanese espionage organization was fomenting unrest and engineering sensational crimes in the United States and its territories.
subfiles.summary: Donisoge attributes unrest in the Philippines, Hawaii, Detroit, and Chicago—and even the Lindbergh kidnapping—to Japanese agents, without presenting evidence. He asks the government to investigate through its secret service and to conceal his identity because he fears retaliation.

subfiles.title: FBI return note for Donisoge-file material
subfiles.from: Department of State Office of Security
subfiles.about: Records the return of the letter and its enclosures to the FBI.
subfiles.summary: The note states that material bearing the file number was returned through the Office of Security. It documents later archival custody rather than the substance of the 1932 allegation.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Japanese tankers in Hawaiian waters
subfiles.about: Indexes a letter alleging that Japanese tankers and intelligence agents appeared near Hawaiian maneuvers and Pan-Pacific gatherings.
subfiles.summary: The note reports that Japanese tankers were habitually observed in Hawaiian waters during military exercises and international events. It suggests that “special visitors” aboard may have been Japanese intelligence agents.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Lieutenant Haraturi and Japanese espionage plans
subfiles.about: Indexes confidential information on Japanese plans and an officer allegedly collecting secrets in the United States.
subfiles.summary: The sheet states that a Japanese officer, Lieutenant Haraturi, supplied information about Japanese plans in the Far East. It alleges that he was then in the United States gathering information for the Japanese espionage service.

subfiles.title: Justice Department transmission of alleged Panama Canal sabotage papers
subfiles.about: Transmits photostats of memoranda and a map apparently describing a plan to dynamite the Panama Canal.
subfiles.summary: The papers were found by Los Angeles cafeteria owner Herbert Wilcox and delivered to the Bureau of Investigation. Dodds says copies were also sent to the Secretary of War.

subfiles.title: English translation of anonymous Los Angeles defense warning
subfiles.about: Claims Japanese residents around Los Angeles and San Pedro were organized to seize local defenses and support a naval attack.
subfiles.summary: The anonymous writer alleges plans to assault the fort at San Pedro, use Terminal Island as a base, mine the Santa Barbara Channel, and destroy petroleum and fleet supplies. The scenario includes ships bringing arms to supporters while the Japanese fleet attacks an unsuspecting American fleet.

subfiles.title: Original Spanish anonymous Los Angeles defense warning
subfiles.about: Spanish original of the warning about an alleged Japanese attack organization in the Los Angeles–San Pedro area.
subfiles.summary: The letter presents the same claims translated on page 27, including seizure of the San Pedro fort, use of Terminal Island, submarine and mine operations, and destruction of naval supplies. Its handwriting and OCR are difficult, but the principal locations and military scenario are identifiable.

subfiles.title: Charge slip for anonymous Los Angeles letter
subfiles.to: Fitter F. / Justice registry, as entered
subfiles.about: Records the temporary charge or circulation of file 894.20211/94 or related material.
subfiles.summary: This is a later administrative form rather than substantive correspondence. Its handwritten entries are partly illegible and appear to identify the person or office to which the document was charged.

subfiles.title: Instruction to Tokyo enclosing Justice Department material on Kasai
subfiles.about: Forwards information concerning alleged activities of Jiuji G. Kasai.
subfiles.summary: The instruction encloses a November 3 Justice Department letter and a communication from Reverend Fred Merrifield. It identifies Kasai as a member of the Tokyo Municipal Assembly's superior council and sends the material for the embassy's information.

subfiles.title: Kasai request for meetings with American officials
subfiles.about: Requests meetings with senior American civilian, naval, and military officials before Kasai's return to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Kasai explains that he represented Tokyo in promoting its bid for the 1940 Olympics and was touring American cities after the Los Angeles games. He seeks frank discussions with Castle, Stimson, and Admiral Pratt to improve Japanese-American understanding and cites cordial sentiments from General Araki and Admiral Okada.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck memorandum of conversation with Kasai
subfiles.to: Division of Far Eastern Affairs file
subfiles.about: Records a three-quarter-hour meeting with Jiuji G. Kasai.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum contains only a brief notation that Kasai called and spoke with Hornbeck. No details of their discussion are supplied.

subfiles.title: Biographical note on Jiuji G. Kasai
subfiles.about: Summarizes Kasai's education, public position, and reputation in Japanese-American relations.
subfiles.summary: The note says Kasai studied at the University of Chicago and Harvard and was prominent in friendship activities. It also records Mr. Salisbury's understanding that the American Embassy in Tokyo disliked Kasai for reasons unknown to him.

subfiles.title: Routing note concerning a possible meeting with Kasai
subfiles.about: Asks whether Hornbeck can see Kasai because Castle will be absent from Washington.
subfiles.summary: The short handwritten note explains that Castle will not be in Washington on the dates Kasai expected to visit. It requests that Hornbeck receive him instead.

subfiles.title: Reply to Kasai concerning Castle's absence
subfiles.about: Advises Kasai that Castle will be absent but Hornbeck will be available to meet him.
subfiles.summary: The Department acknowledges Kasai's October 26 request to call on November 3 or 4. It promises to bring the letter to Hornbeck's attention after his November 1 return to Washington.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Japanese espionage in Aleutian harbors
subfiles.about: Indexes a Navy Department letter on alleged Japanese espionage in Aleutian Island harbors.
subfiles.summary: The sheet redirects readers to file 894.628/94. It contains no details beyond the subject and origin of the referenced letter.

subfiles.title: McCartney forwarding letter concerning Japanese speakers
subfiles.about: Forwards a Japanese Chamber of Commerce circular offering speakers on Japan and Far Eastern questions.
subfiles.summary: McCartney says the communication intimates certain Japanese activities but may be innocent and well meaning. He nevertheless considers it potentially useful for Department files.

subfiles.title: Japanese Chamber of Commerce speaker circular
subfiles.from: Yoshiyasu Kumazawa, Japanese Chamber of Commerce of New York
subfiles.about: Offers Japanese speakers to schools, churches, clubs, and other organizations.
subfiles.summary: Kumazawa presents the service as a means of promoting international goodwill and mutual understanding. Suggested topics include Japanese industry, society, economics, foreign relations, Manchuria, and Far Eastern problems, followed by a form requesting meeting and audience details.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of McCartney's speaker circular
subfiles.about: Acknowledges receipt of the Japanese Chamber of Commerce circular.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck summarizes the circular as an offer by the organization's information bureau to supply speakers on Japan-related subjects. He thanks McCartney for forwarding it.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Japanese information collection in the Aleutians
subfiles.from: Eugene H. Dooman, Department of State
subfiles.about: Indexes a memorandum on Japanese information collection in the Aleutian Islands.
subfiles.summary: The cross-reference points to the Seiji Yoshihara file, 811.79694/52. It identifies collection of information in the Aleutians as the subject.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Yoshihara flight preparations and military information
subfiles.from: Eugene H. Dooman, Department of State
subfiles.about: Indexes a memorandum on military information obtained in preparation for Seiji Yoshihara's flight to the United States.
subfiles.summary: The note points to Seiji Yoshihara file 811.79694/53. It characterizes the referenced information as military and connected with the proposed Japan-to-United States flight.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Nanking despatch on Japanese propaganda
subfiles.about: Indexes a despatch arguing that Japanese propaganda was increasing American support for nonintervention in the Sino-Japanese conflict.
subfiles.summary: The note summarizes the effect as persuading more Americans that Japanese and Chinese people should settle their own quarrel. It directs readers to file 793.94/6036 and despatch D-444.

subfiles.title: Departmental abstract of Nanking propaganda despatch
subfiles.about: Summarizes David Z. T. Yui's and H. W. Liang's observations on American opinion and Japanese propaganda.
subfiles.summary: The abstract says American contacts advised China to continue pressing the League while preparing to recover Manchuria itself. It highlights Liang's contention that Japanese propaganda was effective, internal Chinese disputes were damaging China's case, and Americans favored China but wished to avoid war.

subfiles.title: Peck despatch on Japanese propaganda in the United States
subfiles.from: Willys R. Peck, American Consul General at Nanking
subfiles.about: Transmits synopses of a letter by David Z. T. Yui and an article by H. W. Liang concerning American attitudes toward the Sino-Japanese conflict.
subfiles.summary: Peck reports that Yui's contacts regarded the League and European powers as weak but believed China should continue its diplomatic case while resisting Japan. Liang describes Japanese radio broadcasts, consuls, chambers of commerce, lecturers, and paid American commentators as an effective propaganda network, while stressing that Chinese political divisions caused still greater damage.

subfiles.title: Yui letter on American views of the Sino-Japanese crisis
subfiles.about: Summarizes advice from influential Americans about the League, U.S. treaty obligations, resistance to Japan, and relations with the Soviet Union.
subfiles.summary: Yui argues that the League is ineffective but still valuable as a forum and that the United States will probably limit itself to the Stimson nonrecognition policy. He advises China to resist further invasion, recover Manchuria through its own efforts, avoid a formal war for the moment, support volunteers and the boycott, unify the country, and approach Soviet assistance cautiously.

subfiles.title: Liang article “America and the Far East”
subfiles.about: Analyzes American opinion and Japanese propaganda concerning Manchuria and the Sino-Japanese conflict.
subfiles.summary: Liang says most Americans considered Japan wrong but did not wish to risk war, and he describes propaganda through radio, universities, consulates, chambers of commerce, free lecturers, paid writers, and visiting diplomats. He nevertheless concludes that Chinese warlord and Kuomintang divisions harmed China's standing more than Japanese propaganda, while the Nineteenth Route Army and Manchurian volunteers commanded admiration.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs note on Pacific Coast highway inquiries
subfiles.about: Summarizes an Army report about Japanese inquiries into Pacific Coast highways.
subfiles.summary: The note says the attached San Francisco garrison letter identified several Japanese gathering highway information. It observes that three Japanese Government Railways representatives conducted their inquiries openly and apparently without special significance.

subfiles.title: Ninth Corps Area report on Japanese highway inquiries
subfiles.from: A. M. Jones, Headquarters Ninth Corps Area
subfiles.to: William H. Wilson, War Department G-2
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese note-taking at Fort Columbia and requests for detailed California highway information.
subfiles.summary: Jones says S. Fujii was observed making notes on a new highway tunnel through Fort Columbia. He also reports that K. Inoue, K. Takahashi, and N. Ito of the Japanese Government Railways questioned Los Angeles highway-patrol officials about the state road system for tourism purposes.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs note on alleged aerial photographs
subfiles.about: Introduces an Army memorandum concerning a sailor's story about West Coast aerial photographs held by a Japanese acquaintance.
subfiles.summary: The note identifies the source as a water tender on a Dollar liner and the material as airplane photographs of the West Coast. The division concludes that the story contains nothing of interest for Far Eastern Affairs.

subfiles.title: Philippine Department memorandum on West Coast aerial photographs
subfiles.from: R. T. Taylor, Philippine Department G-2
subfiles.to: Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2, War Department
subfiles.about: Records P. W. Vanciel's claim that a Japanese acquaintance possessed official aerial photographs of the American West Coast.
subfiles.summary: Vanciel said S. Tisakawa showed him photographs being assembled into a mosaic at Kobe and claimed they came through a New York contact from an Army photographer in San Francisco. Taylor regarded Vanciel as presentable but imaginative and noted that he was willing to identify the New York contact to military intelligence.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to a Japanese organizer in Kansas City
subfiles.about: Indexes a letter about a Japanese organizer visiting Kansas City and allegedly causing trouble.
subfiles.summary: The note redirects the reader to file 811.4016/167. It provides no name or further description of the organizer.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Institute of Pacific Relations delegates' propaganda tour
subfiles.about: Indexes a report on Japanese delegates touring to explain Japan's position in the Manchurian affair.
subfiles.summary: The referenced travelers were delegates to an Institute of Pacific Relations conference. Their tour is characterized as propaganda intended to present the Japanese case.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Hornbeck memorandum on Japanese propaganda tour
subfiles.from: Stanley K. Hornbeck, Department of State
subfiles.to: Division of Far Eastern Affairs file
subfiles.about: Indexes reports concerning a tour designed to explain Japan's position and policy.
subfiles.summary: The file note points to memorandum 033.9411/289. Its only substantive description is that the tour concerned Japanese policy and propaganda.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to proposed Japanese private school
subfiles.from: Miller, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Indexes a memorandum suggesting that a proposed Japanese teacher and private school might form part of a broader propaganda program.
subfiles.summary: The note refers to a September 9 inquiry from the Japanese Embassy to the American Council on Education. It suggests the proposal could provide an outlet for Japanese government funds reportedly set aside for propaganda abroad.

subfiles.title: Conversation on Lieutenant Arima and Japanese naval espionage
subfiles.from: Eugene H. Dooman, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Records State and Navy officials' discussion of suspected Japanese efforts to obtain American naval and military information.
subfiles.summary: Commander Flanigan described suspicious factory visits, a Japanese found searching company papers, and Lieutenant T. Arima's contacts with former enlisted men, arguing that the Japanese naval supply inspector's New York office directed espionage. Hornbeck favored gathering decisive evidence and warning the Japanese ambassador and naval attaché rather than relying on prosecution alone; the participants agreed to maintain surveillance and prepare for a possible arrest.

subfiles.title: FBI return note for espionage-file correspondence
subfiles.from: Department of State Office of Security
subfiles.about: Records the return of correspondence and enclosures bearing the file number to the FBI.
subfiles.summary: The page is an archival custody notation rather than substantive intelligence. It documents transfer through the Office of Security in 1957.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to alleged Japanese outreach among Black Americans
subfiles.about: Indexes Reverend G. W. Griffin's belief that Japan fostered the Pacific Movement of the Eastern World among Black Americans.
subfiles.summary: The note characterizes Griffin's claim as an impression rather than an established fact. It redirects the reader to file 811.4016/169.

subfiles.title: Telephone conversation on five Japanese detained at Kearny
subfiles.from: Eugene H. Dooman, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Records Justice Department information about five Japanese suspected of photographing warships and industrial facilities at Kearny.
subfiles.summary: J. Crowley said New Jersey authorities had detained the men but federal agents knew of no applicable charge; only Kuraji Takahashi might face a driver's-license violation. Dooman noted the Navy's interest and contacted Captain Pickens after learning that Captain Collins's New York naval-intelligence office was already informed.

subfiles.title: Herald Tribune clipping on Japanese detained at Kearny
subfiles.about: Reports the detention and questioning of five Japanese men photographing the Kearny Meadows and nearby industrial and transportation sites.
subfiles.summary: The article describes police concern over photographs of railways, the skyway, industrial plants, and shipyards, compounded by Takahashi's use of Yomamoto's driving license and identity. The men said they were Japanese railway engineers studying American industry, while the Japanese consul general was asked to identify them.

subfiles.title: New York Times clipping on Japanese detained at Kearny
subfiles.about: Reports nine hours of police questioning after five Japanese men photographed the Pulaski Skyway and nearby facilities.
subfiles.summary: Police found seven cameras, maps, briefcases, and a golf bag but filed no espionage charge, while federal agents disclaimed involvement. Four men were identified as Japanese Government Railways engineers, and Takahashi's initial use of Yomamoto's name and license prolonged their detention.

subfiles.title: Justice Department transmission of Hart's railway-photography letter
subfiles.from: J. Edgar Hoover, Division of Investigation
subfiles.about: Forwards Edward H. Hart's report of Japanese train passengers photographing railroad bridges.
subfiles.summary: Hoover explains that Military Intelligence sent Hart's January 17 letter to the Division of Investigation. He furnishes a copy to Hornbeck because the observations may interest the State Department.

subfiles.title: Duplicate Justice Department transmission of Hart's letter
subfiles.from: J. Edgar Hoover, Division of Investigation
subfiles.about: Duplicate copy forwarding Hart's observations of Japanese passengers photographing railroad bridges.
subfiles.summary: The text duplicates the received copy on page 75. It identifies Military Intelligence as the intermediary and encloses Hart's letter for possible State Department interest.

subfiles.title: Hart report on systematic photography from trains
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese passengers systematically photographing bridges, railways, factories, power plants, and the Niagara frontier from Pullman trains.
subfiles.summary: Hart says that between 1928 and 1932 groups of four Japanese passengers regularly used still, motion-picture, concealed, and telescopic cameras between Rochester, Buffalo, Niagara Falls, Detroit, and Chicago. He describes photography of bridges, tracks, industrial districts, power facilities, the Peace Bridge, and the Niagara River, and argues that the activity appeared organized and scientific.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Hoover's Hart transmission
subfiles.about: Acknowledges receipt of Hart's letter about Japanese passengers photographing objects from trains.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck summarizes Hart's allegation and thanks Hoover for making it available. The response gives no evaluation of Hart's credibility or proposed action.

subfiles.title: Hawaiian Department report on Masasuke Kobayashi
subfiles.from: James I. Muir, Hawaiian Department G-2
subfiles.to: Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2, War Department
subfiles.about: Reports that Salvation Army officer Masasuke Kobayashi allegedly received a Japanese imperial donation arranged through the Japanese Army.
subfiles.summary: The report identifies Kobayashi as divisional commander of the Japanese branch of the Salvation Army in San Francisco and notes his recent return from Japan. A source considered consistently reliable claimed that the Army recommended him to the emperor and that the resulting 5,000-yen donation actually came from Japanese Army funds.
